extracted.intended_audience: machine-learning researchers, conference organizers, reviewers, area chairs, and developers building AI tools for peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for conference-style peer review in machine learning (ICLR/ICML/NeurIPS-style), plus specifications for AI-assisted review tooling and dataset needs. Covers what reviewers should judge, how to score, and what data/tools are needed to support high-quality review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefly summarize the paper and its contributions in your own words (not a pasted abstract). This is not the place to critique the paper; the authors should generally agree with a well-written summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise description showing your understanding after reading. Summaries should accurately position the contribution relative to prior work and avoid copying the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengths and Weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a thorough assessment of the paper's strengths and weaknesses; frame strengths/weaknesses as reasons you might accept or reject the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Touch on multiple dimensions (quality, clarity, significance, originality). Be concrete: identify specific technical, experimental, or presentation issues and articulate why they matter for acceptance decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality (technical soundness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission technically sound? Are claims well supported (theoretically or empirically)? Are methods appropriate and correctly applied? Is the work complete or a preliminary effort?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for correctness of proofs/derivations, appropriateness of experiments, validity of statistical analysis, possible data leakage or metric misuse. Rate quality on the paper's numerical scale and cite concrete evidence when asserting flaws or strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission clearly written and well organized? Does it provide sufficient information for an expert reader to understand and reproduce results?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give constructive suggestions for improving clarity (sections to expand, notation fixes, line-level edits). Note that clarity is judged by whether an expert could reproduce results; point to specific places where dense notation or missing exposition obstructs understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results impactful for the community? Will other researchers or practitioners likely use these ideas or build on them?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the contribution meaningfully advances understanding, solves an important problem, or offers novel practical value. Indicate the likely breadth/depth of impact and justify with comparisons to prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work provide new insights, deepen understanding, or otherwise advance the topic relative to previous work? Is it a novel method, new theoretical insight, or a valuable empirical/engineering contribution?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality need not be an entirely new method; novel analyses, unique evaluations, or improved properties (efficiency, fairness) count. Explain how the submission differs from prior work and cite relevant references when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric rating scales for Quality/Clarity/Significance/Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign per-dimension numeric ratings (4=excellent, 3=good, 2=fair, 1=poor) for Quality, Clarity, Significance, and Originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ratings to reflect the assessment discussed in Strengths/Weaknesses. Provide justification for each numeric rating tied to specific evidence or analysis in the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall score (1–10) with textual mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an overall score from 1 (Desk Reject) to 10 (Strong Accept). The paper provides explicit mapping: 10 Strong Accept; 9 Accept; 8 Weak Accept; 7 Borderline Accept; 6 Weak Reject; 5 Reject; 4 Strong Reject; 3 Serious Reject; 2 Severe Reject; 1 Desk Reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an overall numeric score that synthesizes the per-dimension ratings and the reviewer's judgment about accept/reject trade-offs. Explain why the paper fits the chosen bucket using stated criteria (technical flaws, significance, reproducibility, ethics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence score (1–5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a confidence level (5=absolutely certain, 1=educated guess) indicating how confident you are in your assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided descriptors: 5 = very familiar and checked details; 4 = confident but not absolute; 3 = fairly confident; 2 = willing to defend but likely gaps; 1 = not in area/educated guess. This helps ACs weigh reviewer input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions and actionable suggestions for authors
rubrics_metrics.description: List and carefully describe ~3–5 questions and suggestions that are actionable, focused on key points that could change your opinion if addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions should be specific and constructive, providing clear guidance on the criteria under which a score could increase or decrease. Aim for concise, actionable items that the rebuttal can address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and negative societal impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the authors have adequately addressed limitations and potential negative societal impacts of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not adequately addressed, provide constructive suggestions for improvement. The guideline encourages rewarding authors for frank discussion of limitations rather than penalizing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage (Report Card dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the review cover key evaluation aspects such as novelty, significance, technical soundness, empirical validation, clarity, and ethics?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated or human review-quality feedback should check coverage and flag missing dimensions (e.g., ethics not discussed). For reviewers, ensure you explicitly comment on each relevant aspect or explain why some aspects are not applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity (Report Card dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the critiques concrete and actionable rather than vague?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer line-level edits, precise experiment recommendations (which datasets/baselines/ablations), and suggested clarifications over generic comments like 'needs more experiments.' Where possible, propose exact experiments or analysis that would resolve concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence backing review claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the review provide evidence for its claims (e.g., quotes, pointers to manuscript sections, references to prior work)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should cite exact manuscript locations (section/figure/equation) or external literature to substantiate assertions. Automated RAV-grounding tools can cross-check and surface counter-evidence; reviewers should treat such outputs as signals requiring human judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructiveness and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the review framed to help authors improve, and is the language professional and respectful?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dismissive or pejorative language; suggest remedial actions and focus on improvement. Automated report cards should evaluate and nudge reviewers toward constructive phrasing when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated Review 'Report Card' (AI feedback on reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: An LLM-generated, multi-dimensional feedback artifact that evaluates a human review across coverage, specificity, evidence, constructiveness, and tone to help reviewers improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report cards can standardize signals for ACs, nudge reviewers to add evidence or actionable steps, and serve as a training curriculum for junior reviewers. They should be used to augment, not replace, human judgment and can be deployed before and after rebuttal phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal reviewer characteristics (benchmark for AI assistants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual 'ideal' reviewer traits an AI assistant should emulate: (1) Comprehensive Knowledge Base, (2) Meticulous Verifiability, (3) Insightful Constructivism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this ideal as a guiding target — comprehensive prior-art awareness, careful factual verification and reproducibility checks, and highly-targeted, actionable feedback — while recognizing current AI limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual verification via Retrieval-Augmented Verification (RAV) and grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-reference paper claims with authoritative literature repositories (Semantic Scholar, arXiv) to suggest citations, flag inconsistencies, and support factual soundness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RAV should explain why retrieved documents support/refute claims. Use RAV outputs as verifiable leads, not final judgments. Note challenges: recency, domain specificity, and false positives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code analysis and reproducibility assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools to parse provided source code and methodology to identify common pitfalls (data leakage, incorrect metric implementation), missing dependencies, or inconsistencies between code and paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated checks can perform sanity checks, surface likely reproducibility issues, and suggest specific fixes; final reproducibility judgment requires human review and potentially running code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content provenance and authenticity detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect AI-generated or heavily AI-assisted content via watermarking, statistical textual features (perplexity/entropy), or other provenance signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current detectors are imperfect (false positives affecting non-native speakers, robustness issues). Use provenance signals as one input among many and accompany them with clear policies and author declarations. Human judgment remains the arbiter.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI decision support for Area Chairs (ACs)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI assistance for AC tasks: synthesizing multiple reviews and rebuttals, summarizing key arguments, highlighting conflicts/gaps, flagging unaddressed concerns, and drafting meta-reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI outputs should highlight contradictions (e.g., Reviewer 1 vs Reviewer 2 on novelty), surface missing evidence, and produce concise summaries. ACs must use these inputs to prioritize investigative attention and retain final judgment responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal best practices (author-response scaffolding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically catalog reviewer points to ensure each is addressed; help authors distinguish misunderstandings vs actual disagreements and craft responses that clarify or present new evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective rebuttals should reply point-by-point, provide concrete additional evidence if available, and be tailored to reviewers' concerns. AI can help map reviewer concerns and propose precise clarifications, but authors should ensure intellectual ownership of scientific content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured data requirements for AI assistant development
rubrics_metrics.description: Key data dimensions needed to build reliable AI assistants: (1) Structured reviewer reasoning for score changes and assertions; (2) Detailed author–reviewer–AC interaction traces with semantic annotations (dialogue acts, argument strength); (3) AC deliberation traces (anonymized/aggregated); (4) Fine-grained annotations linking review statements to manuscript passages and external knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting richer data requires ethical frameworks, privacy-preserving protocols, low-burden interfaces, and community coordination (organizers, OpenReview, funders). Robust AI will need these structured signals rather than coarse scores alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics for AI-assisted review tools (illustrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example evaluation signals used in the paper's experiments: semantic recall of strengths/weaknesses/rebuttal points (LLM-as-judge) and rating prediction accuracy measured by MAE/RMSE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative human evaluation alongside quantitative metrics; semantic coverage (precision/recall against human points) and prediction error are useful baselines but insufficient — richer rationale-aligned metrics and human-in-the-loop validation are required.
